statements.claim: An invisible voice spoke out of the sky and halted the killing: 'do not kill this Jvara. He is worthy of being protected by you.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (12): 'an invisible voice was heard in the sky:—"O Krishna... do not kill this Jvara... he is worthy of being protected by thee"'.

statements.claim: The war was between Krishna and the thousand-armed king Vana, Shiva's devoted servant, and Shiva's creatures fought for Vana — among them Jvara, the fever, who had been created by Hara.
statements.evidence: Arc context of ch. 271-272 (pack chain): Vana is Shiva's protégé whom Shiva defends; Jvara himself says 'Formerly I had been created by Hara the slayer of Tripura' (1.271.29-32).

statements.claim: Jvara entered Krishna's body: Krishna's movements slackened, his steps grew heavy, his hair stood on end, he yawned and sighed without cease and supported himself with one hand on the ground until, after a long time, the great yogi recovered.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (1-5): 'Released from his arms, Jvara... entered into it. Possessed by Jvara Krishna had his movements slackened... his hairs stood erect. He repeatedly sighed and yawned... supported himself by touching the ground... regained his natural state after a long time'.

statements.claim: Krishna created a second, more dreadful Jvara from his own energy, which seized the original by force and dragged it from Krishna's body.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (6-12): 'Purosottama created another for its destruction... created a dreadful Jvara, highly terrible unto creatures. Catching hold, by force, of the former Jvara... presented it before him... driving out that Jvara from his body'.

statements.claim: Krishna threw Jvara down on the earth and was about to tear him into pieces.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (11-12): 'the highly powerful and angry Vāsudeva struck him down on the ground and was about to tear him into pieces'.

statements.claim: Krishna, the lord of the past, present and future and the great preceptor of the world, let Jvara go; Jvara prostrated with bent head and asked to be the only Jvara in the world.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (13-18): 'Hari, the lord of the past, future and present and the great preceptor of the world let Jvara off. Thereupon prostrating himself with bent head... Jvara said... I may be the only Jvara in this world and no one else may flourish'.

statements.claim: Krishna granted the boon and said the counter-Jvara he had created would dissolve in him.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (17-18): 'May you fare well... You will have what you are praying for. As before you will be the only Jvara. May he, whom I have created, dissolve in me'.

statements.claim: Krishna instructed Jvara to divide into three parts — four-legged animals, immobile objects, human beings — with a fourth portion of the third part living among birds, appearing among mankind every day, after two, three and four days.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (19-28): 'divide yourself into three parts. With one do you possess the four-legged animals, with the second the immobile objects and with the third the human beings. And with the fourth portion of your third part you will always live in the midst of the birds... appearing every day, after two days, three days and four days you are to live amongst mankind'.

statements.claim: In trees Jvara would live as the insect and blight that withers leaves, in fruits as Aturya, in lotuses as frost, in the earth as drought/desert, in water as Neelika, in peacocks as the crest, in mountains as mineral, in cows as Khoraka.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (25-27): 'In trees you will live in the shape of an insect and the disease that withers up the leaves... in the fruits... like Aturya disease; in the lotuses like frost, in the earth like a desert, in the water like Neelikā, in the peacocks like the growing of the tuft, in the mountain like mineral and in the cows like Khoraka'.

statements.claim: With Jvara's sight and touch animals would lose their lives; only gods and men could withstand him.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (27-28): 'With your very view and touch the animals will be shorn of their lives. Only gods and men will be able to withstand you'.

statements.claim: Jvara saluted Krishna, said he was created by Hara the slayer of Tripura and, vanquished in battle, had become Krishna's servant.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (29-32): 'blessed I am for thy giving me soverignty over all creatures... Formerly I had been created by Hara the slayer of Tripura... Now vanquished by thee in battle I have become thy servant. Thou art now my master'.

statements.claim: Krishna declared that a man who salutes him and attentively reads the account of the great battle will be freed from fever; Jvara assented and left the battlefield.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (33-37): 'the man, who having saluted me, will attentively read this account... will be freed from fever... Jvara... saluting Krishna, left the battle-field'.

notes: Close to verbatim rendering of Harivamsha 1.271. 'The great battle came to a halt' and 'frost melts into the morning' are connective imagery; no unsupported facts.

statements.claim: Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna, riding Garuda like three fires, dispersed the Danava army with a downpour of arrows, and fire consumed thousands of Danavas.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (1-5): 'riding quickly Vinatā's son, those three (heroes), stationed in the battle-field like three fire-gods... Seated on Garuda's back those highly powerful three heroes assailed and dispersed the Dānava army with a downpour of arrows... consumed thousands of Dānavas'. The trio is Krishna, Baladeva and Pradyumna (1.274: Kartikeya 'drove towards Krishna, Baladeva and Pradyumna').

statements.claim: The survivors scattered, dropping coats of mail, swords, daggers, darts, leathern protectors and axes.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (6-8), Vana's speech enumerates exactly these abandoned items.

statements.claim: Vana shouted his fleeing soldiers back, appealing to their Daitya birth and life with Hara; the Danavas fled anyway, and only the Pramathas stood firm.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (6-11): Vana's rallying words given; 'the Dānavas, beside themselves with fear, paid no heed to them and fled away. Of the soldiers remaining there only the Pramathas stood firm'.

statements.claim: Kumbhanda, Vana's powerful minister and friend, also appealed to the Danavas in vain.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (12): 'Kumbhānda, Vāna's powerful minister and friend' makes the appeal; the Danavas flee before he finishes.

statements.claim: Seeing his soldiers routed, Shiva's eyes reddened with anger, and to protect Vana he stood on his lustrous car; Kartikeya ascended a car burning like fire; Rudra's car drawn by lions, devouring the sky, came like the full moon freed from clouds.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (12-17): 'Siva... had his eyes reddened with anger. And in order to protect Vāna, he stood on his lustrous car... Kumāra too ascended a car burning like... Powerful Rudra, ascending a car drawn by lions... looked like the full-moon freed from clouds'.

statements.claim: The car was surrounded by ghosts with faces of lions, tigers, serpents, horses, camels, asses, peacocks, rams, cats and sheep, variously dressed in bark or animal skins, some dwarfish and grim-visaged, blowing conch-shells and bugles, standing around Shankara.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (17-28): full catalog of the ghostly host given, including 'faces of lions... tigers... serpents... horses... camels... asses... peacocks... rams... cats... sheep', 'put on lion and tiger skins', 'blew conch-shells and bugles', 'stood encircling Shankara'.

statements.claim: Krishna rode Garuda to meet Rudra's car; Hara struck him with hundreds of winged arrows and Hari answered with the weapons given by Indra.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (29-31): 'Krishna, riding Garuda, proceeded to the battle-field... Hara... struck him in anger with hundreds, of winged arrows... Hari too, irate, took up most excellent weapons given by Indra'.

statements.claim: The duel shook the earth, terrified the elephants, scattered mountain summits, set the quarters ablaze, drew inauspicious cries from jackals, and Indra rained blood and fire-brands over the rear of Vana's army.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (32-37): 'the earth shook and the elephants trembled... mountains were covered with the water of streams; some had their summits scattered... quarters, sky and earth were as if all ablaze... dreadful-looking jackals began to emit inauspicious cries... Indra began to send down showers of blood and fire-brands'.

statements.claim: Brahma, knowing Rudra had entered battle, came encircled by celestials; Apsaras, Gandharvas, Yakshas, Vidyadharas, Siddhas and Charanas watched from the sky.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (33-37): 'the Grandfather... came there encircled by the celestials. The Apsaras, Gandharvas, Yakshas, Vidyadharas, Siddhas, and Chāranas, stationed in the sky, began to witness that encounter'.

statements.claim: Vishnu discharged Indra's weapon at Rudra; Hara answered with his dreadful fiery weapon; Krishna and the three other heroes were entirely covered with arrows.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (37+): 'Vishnu discharged Indra's weapon at Rudra... Hara discharged the highly dreadful fiery weapon... Krishna and the three other heroes were entirely covered with arrows'.

notes: 'Half of Vana's army was running, and the rest was burning' is a rhetorical opener (pack: fire consumed thousands, soldiers fled). 'Fire kindled by Krishna's discus': source passage names the fire as engendered by Krishna's arrows, though discus, plough-share and arrows were all used in the same assault — treated as connective detail, core claim (fire consuming thousands) supported. Closing 'sky turned the colour of the end of the world' is atmosphere.

statements.claim: After Krishna and Rudra retired from the field the battle continued, with Kartikeya (Guha) driving his car at Krishna, Baladeva and Pradyumna and striking them with hundreds of sharpened arrows.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (1-4): Janamejaya asks how the battle continued after the two retired; 'Stationed on the car brought by Kumbhānda, Guha (Kārtikeya) drove towards Krishna, Baladeva and Pradyumna and struck them with hundreds of dreadful and sharpened arrows'.

statements.claim: The three heroes, bathed in blood, fought like three fires; Kartikeya countered their three weapons (from Wind-god, Fire-god and Indra) with Shaila, Varuna and Savitri, but the Yadavas devoured all his weapons by illusion.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (4-8): 'Bathed in blood those three gods, like unto three fires, fought with Kumara... he, too, with three weapons, counteracted them and struck the Yadavas with three other weapons, namely Shaila, Vāruna and Sāvitri. They however, devoured, by virtue of their illusory powers, all the weapons'.

statements.claim: Guha, burning with effulgence and biting his lips, took up the dreadful Brahmashira weapon, blazing like a thousand suns and destructive of the world; creatures lost consciousness and the universe bewailed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (8-12): 'Guha... took up the dreadful weapon Brahmashira... endued with the effulgence of a thousand suns and destructive of the world... the creatures lost their consciousness through its warmth... the whole universe bewailed'.

statements.claim: Keshava raised his discus, which clouded the lustre of the Brahmashira as clouds cover the sun, leaving it shorn of power and energy.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (9-12): 'Keshava, the slayer of Keshi, took up his discus... so that discus... clouded... that of Brahmashira weapon... shorn of its lustre, power and energy'.

statements.claim: Kartikeya hurled the golden, bell-set Sakti like the fire of dissolution; it flew into the sky, yawned and moved as if to slay Krishna; the gods feared Krishna would be consumed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (13-16): 'He then discharged... that celestial burning Sakti set with bells... it went up into the sky, yawned and moved about with great force as if desirous of slaying Krishna... the gods... said—"Perhaps Krishna will be consumed"'.

statements.claim: Madhava shouted as if remonstrating and struck the Sakti down to the ground; 'Well done' rose from all sides and Indra with the celestials sent up a leonine shout.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (16-21): 'the highly powerful Mādhava shouted and as if remonstrating struck it down on the ground... arose from all sides exclamations "Well done! Well done!" And Vāsava together with the celestials sent up a leonine shout'.

statements.claim: As Krishna was about to discharge his discus, the beautiful goddess Kottavi, at Mahadeva's mandate, came naked to protect Kumara; Lamva, her eighth portion, stood between them like a golden Sakti.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (22-25): 'When Krishna... was about to discharge his discus, the beautiful Kottavi, at the mandate of Mahādeva, came there naked for protecting Kumāra. The eighth portion of the goddess, Lamvā, intervened between them like a beautiful golden Sakti'.

statements.claim: Krishna was baffled, told Kottavi to fly away, and she refused to put on her cloth for Kumara's protection; Krishna told her to take Guha away and, beholding the naked goddess, put away his discus.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (25-31): 'Krishna was baffled and said... "Fly away soon..."... Kottavi did not put on her cloth for protecting Kumāra... "Take Guha with you and fly away soon..."... beholding that naked goddess... the Lord Hari put away his discus'.

statements.claim: The goddess brought Guha before Hara; seeing Kartikeya released, Vana felt the urge to fight Madhava himself; his ghosts, Yakshas and soldiers fled, only Pramathas remained, and Vana marched out with his Daitya commanders while priests performed benedictory rites.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (28-37): 'the goddess brought Guha before Hara... Vāna came to that place. When he saw Guha released... he felt an inclination for fighting himself with Mādhava... the ghosts, Yakshas and Vāna's soldiers fled away... only Pramathas remained there... his priests and other elderly persons... performed benedictory ceremonies'.

notes: Faithful rendering of Harivamsha 1.274; no unsupported or contradicted claims found.

statements.claim: Vana shouted his boast: Krishna would not escape alive to Dwaraka; being of eight arms he could not fight Vana's thousand arms, which would multiply into a million.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (36-44): Vana's taunt given nearly verbatim: 'You will not escape from me to-day alive to Dwarakā... being of eight arms how you will be able to fight with me who have a thousand arms?... multiply into a million'.

statements.claim: Vana's words travelled like the dreadful waves of an ocean raised by wind, and his angry eyes shone like two suns rising.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (45-48): 'Vāna was thus roaring his words as if travelled all over like the dreadful waves of an ocean raised by the wind... his eyes, filled with anger, shone like two suns rising in the firmament'.

statements.claim: Narada laughed aloud from the palace top, as if sundering the sky, and moved about on his yoga seat, curious to see the battle.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (45-48, 66-76): 'Nārada so laughed aloud that as if the sky was sundered in twain. Seated on a Yoga seat that ascetic, filled with curiosity, moved about on all sides'; later he is 'sitting on the highest top of the palace'.

statements.claim: Krishna replied that heroes do not vaunt, that victory is not won by words, and bade Vana fight and be defeated.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (46-51): Krishna's speech given nearly verbatim, including 'The heroes do not vaunt thus... If by words victory is accomplished in a battle, you would have been no doubt victorious'.

statements.claim: Vana covered Krishna with burning arrows, parighas, nisthringsas, clubs, tomars, shaktis, maces and pattishas; proud thousand-armed Vana fought easily against eight-armed Keshava.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (52-58): 'Vāna, with great care, covered Krishna with burning arrows. With Parighas, Nisthringsas, clubs, Tomaras, Saktis, maces and Pattishas he completely covered Keshava... Although having eight-arms Keshava... fought with thousand-armed Vāna'.

statements.claim: The son of Bali (Vana), enraged at Krishna's superior training, discharged the celestial great weapon Brahma had created for Hiranyakashipu; darkness shrouded the quarters, dreadful omens appeared, and everything passed beyond perception.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (59-62): 'Bali's son was greatly worked up with anger. He then discharged that celestial great weapon... which Brahmā, by his ascetic powers, had formerly created for Hiranyakashipu. When that weapon was shot off all the quarters were enshrouded with darkness... everything was beyond the range of perception'.

statements.claim: The Danavas applauded Vana with 'Well done', the gods cried 'Alas', a dreadful rain of burning arrows fell, and wind, storm and clouds did not move while Keshava was burnt.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (60-62): 'The Dānavas applauded Wāna, saying "Well done! Well done!" and words of exclamations by the gods as "Alas!"... A dreadful downpour of burning arrows was caused... wind, storm or clouds did not move'.

statements.claim: Krishna took up Indra's weapon like inevitable death; the darkness was shorn away, the fire extinguished, the Danavas lost heart, and the gods laughed and roared like lions.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (63-65): 'the divine slayer of Madhu took up Indra's weapon like unto inevitable death... all the worlds were shorn of darkness, the fire was extinguished and the Dānavas completely lost their hearts... the gods began to laugh and roar like lions'.

statements.claim: With thunderbolt-like arrows from the Sarnga bow Krishna sundered Vana's car with horses and standards, then stripped off his crown, coat of mail, bow and shield, struck him on the breast with winged arrows, and Vana swooned.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (78-87): 'with arrows, like unto thunderbolts, shot off his Srānga bow Keshava sundered Vāna's car, with horses and standards, into pieces... separated from Vāna's person his highly lustrous crown, coat of mail, bow and shield... struck him on the breast with winged arrows. Cut to the very quick Vāna lost his consciousness and swooned away'.

statements.claim: Narada rose up clapping from the palace top, blessing his life for witnessing Damodara's prowess and urging Krishna to destroy Diti's son Vana.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (88-95): 'Nārada, who was sitting on the highest top of the palace, rose up with clapping and said "O great fortune!... wonderful prowess of Dāmodara... Destroy soon Diti's son Vāna"'.

statements.claim: The standards themselves fought — the gods' and Danavas' horses clashed, and Garuda and the peacock struck each other with wings, beaks and talons until Garuda seized the peacock's head.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (97-101): 'their standards, encountering each other, fought; so did the horses of the Devas and Dānavas. When Garuda and the peacock fought they struck each other with wings, beaks and talons... Garuda... caught hold of the peacock's head with his beaks'.

notes: Near-verbatim to Harivamsha 1.275 (vv. 36-101). Pack passage is truncated after the peacock fight ('struck him wi[...]'); story's ending (seizing the peacock's head) matches the visible text.

statements.claim: The war had come to Sonitpura because Krishna's grandson Aniruddha had been carried away from Dwaraka and bound with serpent-nooses in Vana's palace.
statements.evidence: Arc background confirmed in Harivamsha 1.276 (pack of DKS_0256): 'The heroic Aniruddha being taken away stealthily the city of Dwārakā is filled with anxiety... waiting, bound with serpents, in the female appartment'; Aniruddha is Pradyumna's son, hence Krishna's grandson.

statements.claim: Garuda and the great peacock of Vana's banner fought in the air, striking with wings, beaks and talons, until the eagle caught the peacock's head in his beak.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (97-101): 'When Garuda and the peacock fought they struck each other with wings, beaks and talons... Garuda... caught hold of the peacock's head with his beaks'.

statements.claim: Vana rose again (the second time that day) after his chariot, horses and standards had been shattered by Krishna's Sarnga bow and his crown, mail, bow and shield lay scattered; he came on with a thousand armed hands.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (82-87, continued after truncation per evt_0356 summary): the car is sundered and arms stripped by Sarnga arrows (vv. 82-87); the canonical summary for evt_0356 has Krishna and Vana facing off again when the goddess intercedes.

statements.claim: Vana roared the boast again ('You will not escape me alive to Dwaraka... Being of eight arms, how will you fight me, who have a thousand?... arms multiply into a million') and Krishna answered that heroes do not vaunt.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (36-51): the full boast and Krishna's reply are in the pack passage (same chapter as this story's event).

statements.claim: Vana loosed the great weapon Brahma had created for Hiranyakashipu, darkening all quarters; Krishna took up Indra's weapon, dispelling the darkness; Vana then buried Krishna under maces and spears, and Krishna felled him with winged arrows so that he lost consciousness.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (59-65, 78-87): the Brahma-for-Hiranyakashipu weapon, its darkness, Indra's weapon counter, the maces/pattishas barrage and the winged-arrow swoon are all in the pack passage.

statements.claim: Narada rose up clapping on the palace roof, hailing Damodara's prowess and urging the destruction of Diti's son Vana.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (88-95): Narada's praise from the palace top given in the pack passage.

statements.claim: When the discus was in Krishna's hand, the goddess Kottavi (Lamva) stepped between them unclothed, saying she had conferred a boon on Vana to protect him and would not see it broken.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt for evt_0356 (Harivamsha 1.275): 'Lamvā... appeared naked before Vasudeva... said:—"...I conferred on him a boon saying that I would protect him"'.

statements.claim: Krishna vowed to cut off Vana's thousand arms but spare his life — Vana would live with only two arms; the discus then cut off the arms, and Vana stood alive with two, the boon and vow both honoured.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt for evt_0356 (Harivamsha 1.275): Krishna said 'I will forsooth cut off to-day his thousand arms... Your son will live even if Vāna has two arms'; index summary: 'Krishna vows to cut off Vana's thousand arms, leaving only two, while sparing his life'.

statements.claim: Shiva, who had once promised Vana his protection, was watching the battlefield.
statements.evidence: Lead-in to evt_0357 (pack excerpt, Harivamsha 1.275): Mahadeva says 'I have promised Vāna protection'; DKS_0255 recounts the intercession.

notes: Story opens by re-narrating the tail of the ch. 275 duel (boast, Brahma/Indra weapons, winged-arrow swoon, Narada's praise) that DKS_0253 already covered — the shared pack passage is truncated so the arm-cutting scene itself is supported only by the index/excerpt summary of evt_0356, which the story matches. No contradicted or unsupported claims.

statements.claim: Vana stood with only two hands left after his thousand arms fell; Krishna's discus was poised to end him when Shiva spoke.
statements.evidence: Follows evt_0356 (arms cut to two, life spared pending Shiva's plea) and evt_0357 excerpt: Krishna says 'I withdraw my discus. At thy request Vāna will live'.

statements.claim: Shiva said he had promised Vana protection long ago, that Vana had worshipped him, and bade Krishna desist and let him live.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.275): 'Mahadeva said:—"...I have promised Vāna protection... desist"'.

statements.claim: Krishna withdrew his discus, saying: 'I withdraw my discus... At your request, Vana will live.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.275): 'Krishna... "I withdraw my discus. At thy request Vāna will live"'.

statements.claim: Nandi, Shiva's bull, bade Vana dance before the lord, and the two-armed Vana danced; Shiva was pleased and told Vana to ask a boon.
statements.evidence: Index summary evt_0357: 'the armless Vana, bidden by Nandi, dances before Shiva and receives boons'; pack excerpt: 'Vāna... began to dance... Mahādeva... said:—"I am pleased with you... pray for a boon"'.

statements.claim: The boons made Vana Mahakala, chief of the Pramathas, Shiva's chosen attendant, and he left in the company of Rudra.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.276 (opening, in pack of DKS_0256): 'Having thus obtained a number of boons Vāna was highly pleased. And having attained to the dignity of Mahākala he went with Rudra'; index summary evt_0357: 'becoming the Pramatha chief Mahakala'.

notes: Story honestly flags that the sources do not set down Vana's exact request in full — consistent with the pack (excerpt + index give the dance, the boon and the Mahakala outcome; ch. 275 passage itself is truncated before this scene). 'Nandi at Shiva's side', murmurs and dust settling are connective. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: The war began when Usha, daughter of Vana, carried away Aniruddha, Krishna's grandson, who was bound with serpent-nooses in her father's palace.
statements.evidence: Arc background; Harivamsha 1.276 passage (this pack): 'The heroic Aniruddha being taken away stealthily the city of Dwārakā is filled with anxiety... waiting, bound with serpents, in the female appartment'; the Usha-Aniruddha match is the arc of the corpus chain.

statements.claim: The serpents binding Aniruddha left his body like arrows the moment Garuda's shadow fell; Aniruddha saluted Krishna, Balabhadra, Garuda and his father Pradyumna, and Usha saluted bashfully.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.276 (8-17): 'Seeing Garuda, all the huge serpents... at once left him... dropped on the ground as arrows... Aniruddha saluted the highly powerful and illustrious Balabhadra... bowed unto the great Garuda... approached his father Pradyumna and saluted him. Ushā too... with bashfulness she also bowed'.

statements.claim: Narada asked Krishna to celebrate a marriage acquired by prowess for Aniruddha and to see the exchange of jokes between the bridal parties; the wedding was celebrated with Apsaras cutting jokes and Gandharvas singing.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.276 (18-28): Narada's request quoted; 'the Apsaras began to cut diverse jokes with him. The Gandharvas sang melodious and auspicious songs and the Apsaras danced'.

statements.claim: Krishna gave Vana's kingdom to Kumbhanda, who had asked only for safety, and promised him protection.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.276 (24-28): Kumbhānda seeks refuge; Krishna: 'You will now become the king of this kingdom. I confer this kingdom on you. Live you for ever under my protection'.

statements.claim: Kumbhanda told Krishna that Vana had cows in Varuna's keeping whose nectar-like milk makes a man highly powerful, invincible in battle and immortal.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.276 (34-35): 'Vāna has some cows in charge of Varuna. They give nectar-like milk, drinking which a man becomes highly powerful and invincible in battle'; pack excerpt: 'the kine of Vāna... drinking whose milk a man becomes immortal'.

statements.claim: The celestial kine were sought for Satyabhama; Krishna, his mind filled with joy, set out at once; Baladeva, Krishna, Pradyumna and Aniruddha mounted Garuda, who rose uprooting trees and shaking the earth.
statements.evidence: Index summary evt_0359: 'Seeking Vana's celestial kine in Varuna's charge for Satyabhama'; Harivamsha 1.276 (35, 97-100): 'Hari's mind was filled with joy... Baladeva, Krishna, the highly powerful Pradyumna and energetic Aniruddha sat on Garuda's back. Uprooting the trees and shaking the earth, Garuda... went on'.

statements.claim: Varuna's army came out to keep the kine and was routed by the high-souled Keshava.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.276): 'Varuna's... army... were all routed by the high-souled Keshava'.

statements.claim: Varuna loosed the Varuna-weapon and the sea rose against Krishna; Krishna met it with the Vaishnava weapon, and with its energy the water itself was ablaze, consuming the Varuna-weapon.
statements.evidence: Index summary evt_0359: 'Krishna routs Varuna's army and battles Varuna, whose Varuna-weapon is consumed by Krishna's Vaishnava weapon'; pack excerpt: 'with the energy of Vaishnava weapon that water was ablaze'.

statements.claim: Weaponless and ruined, Varuna still did not yield the cows.
statements.evidence: Consistent with evt_0360 (next story): Varuna pleads that he promised Vana never to give away the kine — the pack excerpt of DKS_0257 quotes his refusal.

notes: Opening paragraphs recap the Aniruddha rescue/wedding from the same ch. 276 passage (supported). 'City had fallen' and battle-shore description are connective. Satyabhama motive comes from the index summary, not the (truncated) passage body — noted but treated per the summary as intended reading.

statements.claim: Varuna stood in his ruined domain with his army routed and his great weapon consumed, yet still refused to surrender the cows.
statements.evidence: Continuation of evt_0359 (pack excerpt: Varuna's army routed by Keshava, Varuna-weapon consumed by Vaishnava weapon) plus evt_0360 excerpt: Varuna refuses to give away the kine.

statements.claim: Varuna said he had promised Vana long ago that if he lived he would never give the kine away, and would not break his word even to save himself.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.276): 'Varuna said... "I had formerly promised, that if alive I would never give away these kine"'.

statements.claim: Krishna, honouring Varuna's truthfulness, released the cows and Varuna, saying: 'You are truthful... Therefore, to please you, I let Vana's cows go free. And you too are released.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.276): 'Krishna... said:—"...you are truthful and therefore for pleasing you I let loose Vāna's cows. And you too are released"'.

statements.claim: The battle ended in a kept promise rather than conquest.
statements.evidence: Frame commentary over the supported resolution; the pack records the release but not this editorializing.

statements.claim: Krishna, Baladeva, Pradyumna and Aniruddha returned to Dwaraka on Garuda, and the celestial kine came to graze in the fields of the Yadava capital, where the rejoicing citizens welcomed them home.
statements.evidence: Index summary evt_0360: 'Krishna... releases both Varuna and the cows and returns to Dwarka amid the rejoicing citizens'; Harivamsha 1.276: the same four ride Garuda back (v. 97-100); kine settling in Dwarka follows the Satyabhama motive of evt_0359.

statements.claim: The tale of the fallen thousand arms, the dance before Shiva and the burning sea spread through the city.
statements.evidence: Recap of earlier events (evt_0356/0357/0359), all pack-supported; framing only.

notes: Krishna's dialogue and Varuna's plea are near-verbatim from the pack excerpt. The story's reconciliation (release the cows yet they come to Dwarka) goes slightly beyond the excerpt, which records only the release and the return; consistent with the intended reading (kine sought for Satyabhama, evt_0359 index). Citizens' rejoicing, lamps and children are connective.
